entry.title: Reaching goals from offline data: GTRL and the goal-representation question

link.title: Reaching goals from offline data: GTRL and the goal-representation question

entry.content:
Can an agent learn to reach any goal, across long horizons, using nothing but a fixed dataset of past experience? That is the question behind our newest line of work in offline goal-conditioned reinforcement learning (GCRL). In September 2026 we released two preprints on it.

At a glance

  • Status: Ongoing research
  • Area: Robot learning, reinforcement learning
  • Papers: GTRL (arXiv 2026) · Do Better Goal Representations Improve GCRL? (arXiv 2026)

GTRL: grounding divide-and-conquer with temporal differences

Divide-and-conquer value learning scales to long horizons by joining two shorter segments at a subgoal. It has two blind spots, though. Under stochastic dynamics, its base case ends up valuing the luckiest trajectories in the data. And a state–goal pair that no logged trajectory connects never receives a value update at all.

GTRL (Grounded Transitive RL) fixes both by adding a one-step temporal-difference (TD) target to the composition. Over a single step TD is correct: its target averages over successor states and needs no subgoal. With that addition every pair receives an update, and the composition still carries the long horizon. GTRL also corrects the bias introduced by hindsight relabeling by reweighting each goal according to how reachable it was from other successors. Across nineteen OGBench tasks spanning stochastic, deterministic, and stitching environments, GTRL achieves the highest average success rate.

Abdul Monaf Chowdhury, MD Sameer Iqbal Chowdhury, Shifat E Arman, Md Mehedi Hasan. arXiv:2609.33259

Is the goal representation really the bottleneck?

Much recent GCRL research focuses on better ways to encode goals, using temporal distance, occupancy, or controllability. We asked how much that actually matters.

We built an exact temporal-distance goal representation in deterministic mazes, then systematically corrupted it while keeping the downstream learner fixed. Large changes in goal-representation quality produced almost no change in performance. The same interventions applied to the agent’s current state, however, more than doubled success. The state pathway is the real bottleneck. Building on that finding, simple random Fourier positional encodings of the state substantially improve performance on the hardest navigation tasks, with no map information and no change to the objective.

Syed Nazmus Sakib, Abdul Monaf Chowdhury, Nafiul Haque, Shifat E Arman, Md Mehedi Hasan. arXiv:2609.39901

What’s next

Code for both papers will be released soon. In parallel, lab members are working on long-horizon, multi-task embodied manipulation, which is where better offline value learning pays off most.
entry.summary: Can an agent learn to reach any goal, across long horizons, using nothing but a fixed dataset of past experience? That is the question behind our newest line of work in offline goal-conditioned reinforcement learning (GCRL). In September 2026 we released two preprints on it.

entry.title: PlantPhenoBot: robotics for plant phenotyping
entry.content:
PlantPhenoBot is the lab’s newest funded project. It is a robotics project for plant phenotyping, the measurement of plant traits such as growth, architecture, and stress response. The project began in May 2026 under a UGC–DU research grant, in collaboration with Gazipur Agricultural University.

At a glance

  • Status: Ongoing (started 7 May 2026)
  • Funding: UGC–DU research grant
  • Collaborator: Gazipur Agricultural University
  • Principal investigator: Dr. Md Mehedi Hasan
  • Area: Robotics, plant phenomics

Why phenotyping needs robots

Crop breeders choose new varieties by measuring traits plant by plant: how fast a plant grows, how many spikes or bolls it sets, and how it copes with drought, heat, or disease. Done by hand, this is slow, subjective, and hard to scale beyond a few plots. Robots and imaging platforms can collect the same measurements automatically and consistently, at far higher throughput. This is high-throughput phenotyping, and it is one of the main bottlenecks between plant science and better crops.

Building on years of phenotyping work

PlantPhenoBot draws on a long line of AVIS Lab research in plant phenomics:

  • Wheat spike detection and segmentation. Dr. Hasan’s 2018 Plant Methods paper on detecting wheat spikes with CNNs, followed by WheatSpikeNet (Frontiers in Plant Science, 2023) and a multi-stage CNN for spike analysis (DUJASE, 2023).
  • Seedling monitoring. Cotton seedling growth-stage classification from UAV and ground-level imagery, with a biologically grounded Composite Stress Index (Smart Agricultural Technology, 2025).
  • Disease diagnosis. PlantCareNet (Plant Methods, 2025) and SugarcaneShuffleNet, a very fast model for on-device diagnosis of sugarcane leaf diseases.
  • Expert-style reasoning. PlantInquiryVQA (Findings of ACL 2026), a benchmark that tests whether multimodal models can question a leaf image the way a botanist does.

We’ll post updates here as the project progresses.

entry.title: Thinking Like a Botanist: PlantInquiryVQA in Findings of ACL 2026

link.title: Thinking Like a Botanist: PlantInquiryVQA in Findings of ACL 2026

entry.content:
Our paper Thinking Like a Botanist: Challenging Multimodal Language Models with Intent-Driven Chain-of-Inquiry is published in Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: ACL 2026. It introduces PlantInquiryVQA, a benchmark that asks whether multimodal AI can reason about a plant the way an expert does, one targeted question at a time.

At a glance

  • Venue: Findings of ACL 2026
  • Dataset: 24,950 expert-curated plant images · 138,068 question–answer pairs
  • Links: ACL Anthology · arXiv

The problem: one question is not a diagnosis

A botanist examining a diseased leaf does not answer a single question and stop. They spot visual cues, form a hypothesis about what is going on, and ask follow-up questions that adapt to the species, the symptoms, and the severity. That structured probing is what makes their diagnoses accurate and their treatment advice safe. Vision-language models, however, are almost always evaluated on single-turn question answering.

What we built

  • Chain of Inquiry. A framework that models a diagnosis as an ordered sequence of questions and answers, each conditioned on grounded visual cues and an explicit diagnostic intent.
  • PlantInquiryVQA. 24,950 expert-curated plant images and 138,068 question–answer pairs, annotated with visual grounding, severity labels, and domain-specific reasoning templates.

What we found

Top-tier multimodal large language models describe visual symptoms reasonably well, but they struggle with safe clinical reasoning and accurate diagnosis. Guiding them through structured, question-led inquiry significantly improves diagnostic correctness, reduces hallucination, and makes their reasoning more efficient. We hope PlantInquiryVQA helps the community train diagnostic agents that reason like expert botanists rather than act as static classifiers.

Syed Nazmus Sakib, Nafiul Haque, Shahrear Bin Amin, Hasan Muhammad Abdullah, Md. Mehedi Hasan, Mohammad Zabed Hossain, Shifat E. Arman.

It introduces PlantInquiryVQA, a benchmark that asks whether multimodal AI can reason about a plant the way an expert does, one targeted question at a time.

entry.title: Flying with one camera: vision-language models for UAV navigation

link.title: Flying with one camera: vision-language models for UAV navigation

entry.content:
Most autonomous drones avoid obstacles with expensive sensors, a prebuilt map, or both. Our UAV research asks how far a drone can get with a single monocular camera and a vision-language model (VLM) that reasons about what it sees. The first answer, VLM-Nav, was published in PLOS One in April 2026. A sim-to-real follow-up is now available as a preprint.

At a glance

  • Status: Ongoing research
  • Area: Autonomous UAVs, vision-language models
  • Papers: VLM-Nav (PLOS One, 2026) · Cross-modal benchmarking with sim-to-real evaluation (SSRN preprint, 2026)

VLM-Nav: mapless navigation from monocular vision

VLM-Nav converts each RGB frame from the drone into a depth map using DepthAnything-V2, a zero-shot depth estimator. A VLM (the study explores Gemini-flash and GPT-4o) reads the depth map, detects nearby obstacles, and proposes an avoidance manoeuvre. A small fully connected network then combines the VLM’s output with the UAV’s heading relative to its target and picks the next action. No map is needed, and the hardware is cheap.

Gobinda Chandra Sarker, AKM Azad, Sejuti Rahman, Md Mehedi Hasan. This builds on Gobinda’s MSc thesis on monocular, depth-based UAV navigation in 3D terrain (2024).

From simulation to a real quadrotor

The follow-up study moves the reasoning off the aircraft. The UAV streams live video to a ground station, which fuses monocular depth with a VLM and sends back discrete MAVLink commands.

  • In simulation: six contemporary VLMs were benchmarked across nine factorially controlled Unity–ROS 2 scenes, covering 265 episodes and 3,383 logged decisions.
  • In flight: three cloud VLMs and a non-learning heuristic baseline were flown on a Pixhawk 6C quadrotor, with 1,568 decisions recorded for each.

Every reported proportion comes with a Wilson 95% confidence interval and a significance test. The work grew out of the 2025 student project Advancing UAV Flight and Obstacle Avoidance with Cross-Modal Deep Learning Integration.

Abyead Zarif Hassan, Samiha Tarannum Noor, AKM Azad, Md Mehedi Hasan.

Earlier UAV work

Earlier UAV work in the lab focused on aerial perception. Projects included object and intrusion detection from UAVs, and human-action recognition from drone video with FFT-UAVNet (2023) and U-ActionNet (IEEE Access, 2024).

The first answer, VLM-Nav, was published in PLOS One in April 2026. A sim-to-real follow-up is now available as a preprint.

entry.title: Explainable AI for histological cancer detection

link.title: Explainable AI for histological cancer detection

entry.content:
Deep learning can now classify microscopic tissue images with high accuracy, but pathologists rarely trust a model that cannot show why it reached a decision. This project builds cancer-detection models that are both accurate and interpretable. It is funded by the Ministry of Science and Technology (MOST) and runs in collaboration with Bangladesh Medical University (BMU).

At a glance

  • Project: Enhancing Histology Cancer Cell Detection: Deep Learning Model Interpreted with eXplainable AI (XAI) for Microscopic Tissue Image Analysis
  • Status: Ongoing (started 19 October 2025)
  • Funding: Ministry of Science and Technology (MOST), Bangladesh
  • Collaborator: Bangladesh Medical University (BMU)
  • Principal investigator: Dr. Md Mehedi Hasan

The approach

The project builds on a 2024 student research project of the same name by Shamaeta Paul Gupta and Apurba Roy. The resulting framework (preprint):

  • combines an ensemble of three pretrained CNNs: ResNet50, VGG16, and InceptionV3;
  • uses a 4× super-resolution step to sharpen tissue images before classification, which improved accuracy by 1–10% (ResNet50 96.21%, VGG16 92.14%, InceptionV3 96.42%);
  • explains each prediction with Grad-CAM, SHAP, and LIME, so clinicians can see which regions and features drove the decision.

The MOST-funded project continues this work with clinical collaborators at BMU.

Related medical-AI work in the lab

  • Explainable vision-language models for medical reports. An ongoing MPhil project (Md Julhas Hossain) is building a framework that automatically interprets diagnostic medical reports and explains them to patients.
  • Bone health from X-rays. IG-CNN (IEEE ICECTE 2026) and a follow-up preprint apply information-geometric deep learning to knee osteoporosis diagnosis.
  • Biosignals. FA-EEGNet classifies stroke-rehabilitation movements from EEG, and a 2025 student project explored an EEG-actuated bionic hand.

This project builds cancer-detection models that are both accurate and interpretable. It is funded by the Ministry of Science and Technology (MOST) and runs in collaboration with Bangladesh Medical University (BMU).

entry.title: Inter-University Robotics and Hackathon Competition
entry.content:
Between May 2024 and August 2025, Dr. Md Mehedi Hasan was part of the Inter-University Robotics and Hackathon Competition, an ICT-funded project bringing robotics students from different universities together.

At a glance

  • Status: Completed (May 2024 – August 2025)
  • Funding: ICT (Government of Bangladesh)
  • Area: Robotics education and outreach

Why it matters

Competitions like this have students design, build, and program real systems under time pressure. It’s one of the best ways to learn robotics outside the classroom. If you’re a student who wants to take that experience into research, see Join Us.

entry.title: SmartPDE: forecasting plant disease for smart agriculture

link.title: SmartPDE: forecasting plant disease for smart agriculture

entry.content:
Plant diseases cut yields and threaten food security, and in many places farmers spot them only once the damage is visible across a field. SmartPDE set out to use deep learning not only to recognize plant diseases but to model how they spread and to forecast outbreaks, so that farmers can act earlier.

At a glance

  • Project: SmartPDE: Deep Learning Based Plant Disease Epidemiology and Forecasting for Smart Agriculture
  • Status: Completed (November 2023 – October 2024)
  • Funding: University Grants Commission (UGC), Bangladesh
  • Principal investigator: Dr. Md Mehedi Hasan
  • Area: Precision agriculture

What came out of it

SmartPDE was also the subject of Muhaiminul Islam’s MSc thesis (2024). Closely related work from the same period produced PlantCareNet, published in Plant Methods in 2025. PlantCareNet is an end-to-end diagnostic system: a CNN classifies diseases from leaf images, and the system then gives two kinds of advice, automated suggestions based on the detected symptoms and expert-guided recommendations for prevention and treatment.

The lab’s plant-health work has continued since, with SugarcaneShuffleNet for on-device diagnosis of sugarcane leaf diseases and the current PlantPhenoBot project.

SmartPDE set out to use deep learning not only to recognize plant diseases but to model how they spread and to forecast outbreaks, so that farmers can act earlier.

entry.title: IHABOT2: a teleoperated hospital assistance robot

link.title: IHABOT2: a teleoperated hospital assistance robot

entry.content:
Infectious diseases spread fastest where people are in close contact, and hospitals are among those places. IHABOT2 was a robotics project to develop a teleoperated, intelligent hospital-assistance robot. Its aim was to help fight contagion by reducing how often doctors must be in direct contact with patients.

At a glance

  • Status: Completed (July 2023 – June 2024)
  • Funding: University Grants Commission (UGC), Bangladesh
  • Principal investigator: Dr. Md Mehedi Hasan
  • Area: Robotics, healthcare

Why it matters

A robot that can carry out routine tasks at the bedside under remote control helps keep clinicians safer during outbreaks. IHABOT2 is part of the lab’s broader work on robots that assist people. That work includes the sensor-controlled bionic arm and ADANet motion-acquisition framework for gesture-based assistive interfaces (IEEE Access, 2025), and a review of robot-assisted training for children with autism (Journal of Intelligent & Robotic Systems, 2023).

entry.title: Deep learning for neurodegenerative disease diagnosis using image memorability

link.title: Deep learning for neurodegenerative disease diagnosis using image memorability

entry.content:
Neurodegenerative diseases such as Alzheimer’s are hard to detect early, when intervention helps most. This MOST-funded project investigated deep-learning-driven, automated diagnosis of neurodegenerative diseases using image memorability, a measurable property of how well images are remembered.

At a glance

  • Project: Deep Learning-Driven Automated Diagnosis of Neurodegenerative Diseases Using Image Memorability
  • Status: Completed (January 2022 – January 2023)
  • Funding: Ministry of Science and Technology (MOST), Bangladesh
  • Principal investigator: Dr. Md Mehedi Hasan
  • Area: Medical AI

Where it led

This was one of the lab’s first funded medical-AI projects at the University of Dhaka. The lab’s medical work has since grown into explainable AI for histological cancer detection, EEG-based rehabilitation and brain–computer interfaces, and bone-health assessment from X-rays.

This MOST-funded project investigated deep-learning-driven, automated diagnosis of neurodegenerative diseases using image memorability, a measurable property of how well images are remembered.
